MCP Config Risk Check

Paste an mcp.json, claude_desktop_config.json, or any MCP server config and get every risky pattern flagged in seconds -- broad filesystem/shell access, secrets hardcoded instead of referenced from the environment, missing version pins, and duplicate tool names across servers.

Mechanical checks, not a security audit. This tool never contacts a server, a registry, or a vulnerability database -- it only looks at the text you paste and flags structural patterns in it. A finding is something worth a human look, not a verdict, and a clean result is not a safety guarantee.

1. Paste your config

Accepts the Claude Desktop / Claude Code {"mcpServers": {...}} shape, VS Code's {"servers": {...}} shape, a bare name-to-config object, or an array of server entries. Nothing here is uploaded -- everything runs in this page.

Findings

0server(s) parsed
0high-severity
0medium-severity

Paste a config above, or load the example, to see findings.

    Usage is optional, stays in this browser, and counts only that an audit ran or a summary was copied. Nothing you paste -- no config contents, server names, or findings -- is ever recorded, uploaded, or sent to an analytics service. Uncheck to turn it off. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control disable counting automatically.

    Common questions

    What config formats does this tool accept?

    The Claude Desktop / Claude Code shape ({"mcpServers": {...}}), the VS Code shape ({"servers": {...}}), a bare object of server name to config with no wrapper key, and a plain array of server entries. If an entry also carries a "tools" list (as a captured manifest export would), the duplicate-tool-name check runs against it too.

    Does this tool contact my MCP servers, a registry, or a vulnerability database?

    No. It never makes a network request of its own. It only looks at the text you paste, entirely in your browser, and flags structural patterns in it — it does not verify a package's actual published version, scan its code, or know whether a server is currently compromised.

    Is a flagged finding proof that a server is unsafe?

    No. Every finding is a structural pattern worth a human look, not a verdict. A shell-launching server or an unpinned package can be entirely intentional and fine for your setup; a config with zero findings is not a guarantee of safety either — it only means none of this tool's mechanical checks fired.

    How is this different from a tool that diffs two MCP manifests over time?

    This tool looks at a single, current config — the file your client reads to launch each server — and flags risk patterns in it right now. MCP Supply-Chain Watch instead compares two captured tool manifests to show what changed between them (a tool added, removed, or given a description with model-directed instruction language). Both are useful and answer different questions: this one asks "is today's launch config risky?"; that one asks "what changed since I last approved this server?"

It is not a security audit, and it does not replace reviewing your own config and each server's source before trusting it.     Privacy. Everything runs client-side in your browser. The config you paste, and every finding this tool produces, never leaves your device -- there is no upload, no server-side processing, and no third-party analytics vendor.

    Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, export your inputs and run it yourself.

    Tracking drift between two connected-server snapshots over time instead? See MCP Supply-Chain Watch. Sizing an LLM API bill instead of auditing a config? See the LLM API Pricing Calculator. Checking a pasted file for hidden or invisible Unicode instead of a launch config's structure? See Hidden Unicode Check. Linting a SKILL.md agent-skill manifest instead of a server launch config? See Skill Manifest Check. Checking Claude Code's own settings.json hooks and permissions instead of an MCP server's launch config? See Claude Code Settings Check. Checking a Claude Code subagent definition's tools/model fields instead of a server launch config? See Claude Code Subagent Check. Checking a Claude Code hook's command text for dangerous shapes instead of a server launch config? See Claude Code Hooks Security Check.

vs-mcp-scan.html.text:
← MCP Config Risk Check

MCP Config Risk Check vs. MCP-Scan

Related tools, different layers. MCP-Scan connects to the servers in your MCP client configuration and judges their live tool descriptions for poisoning, shadowing, and rug pulls. This tool never connects to anything -- it reads the launch config itself and flags what you are about to grant a server before it ever starts.

What each tool is for

MCP-Scan (github.com/invariantlabs-ai/mcp-scan, run with uvx mcp-scan@latest) is an open-source security scanner from Invariant Labs. Per its own documentation, it reads your MCP client configuration to find configured servers, connects to each one, retrieves its live tool descriptions, and scans them — combining local checks with a call to Invariant's own Guardrailing API — for tool poisoning, prompt injection in tool descriptions, cross-origin tool-shadowing attacks, and rug pulls (a tool's description changing after you already approved it). Its proxy mode can also monitor live MCP traffic.

This checker reads the same kind of config file but never connects to a server at all: it parses the command, args, and env block for each entry and flags structural risk in the grant itself — broad filesystem or shell access, an API key or token hardcoded in the config instead of referenced from the environment, a launched package or image with no version pin, and a tool name that shadows another server's when a tool list is present. It runs entirely in your browser: no install, no account, and no network call of its own.

QuestionMCP-ScanMCP Config Risk Check
What it readsLive tool descriptions, retrieved by connecting to each configured serverThe launch config itself — command, args, env — nothing is run or connected to
Network callsConnects to each MCP server, plus a call to Invariant's Guardrailing APINone. Everything runs client-side in your browser
Installuvx mcp-scan@latest or an npx equivalentNone — a web page
What a finding meansA tool's description looks like poisoning, shadowing, or a post-approval rug pullThe config grants broad access, hardcodes a secret, skips a version pin, or shadows a tool name
When it can runAfter the server is reachable and runningBefore you ever launch anything — on the config text alone

Why the launch grant is a different question from the tool description

A tool-description scan judges what a server says about itself once it is already running with whatever access the config gave it. That access is decided earlier, in the same config file MCP-Scan reads to find the server in the first place — and nothing about a clean tool-description scan tells you whether that grant was broader than the job needed, whether a token is sitting in the file in plain text, or whether the launched package is pinned to a version at all. A server can pass every tool-poisoning check and still have been launched with filesystem access it never uses, a hardcoded key that a version-controlled copy of the config would leak, or no pin on a package that could change under it on the next install.

Neither question replaces the other. A perfectly scoped, pinned, secret-free launch grant says nothing about whether the tools that server exposes are honestly described, and a clean tool-poisoning scan says nothing about whether the grant itself was tighter than it needed to be.

When to reach for MCP-Scan instead

If you want to know whether a server's tool descriptions are trying something — injected instructions, a description that silently changed since you approved it, a name that shadows another server's tool once both are connected — that is what MCP-Scan is built to answer, and it needs to actually connect to find out. This tool does not attempt that: it never reads a tool description and has no opinion on whether one is honest.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or MCP-Scan?

Different layers of the same problem. MCP-Scan (uvx mcp-scan@latest, from Invariant Labs) connects to each server named in your MCP client configuration, retrieves its live tool descriptions, and judges them for tool poisoning, prompt injection, cross-origin tool shadowing, and rug pulls -- combining local checks with a call to Invariant's own Guardrailing API. This tool never connects to anything: it reads the launch config itself and flags structural risk in what you are about to grant -- broad filesystem or shell access, an API key or token hardcoded instead of referenced from the environment, a package or image with no version pin, and a tool name that shadows another server's. If you want to know what a server's tools actually say once it is running, MCP-Scan is built for exactly that. If you want to know what your config is about to hand that server before it ever starts, this is the narrower, offline question this tool answers.

Isn't a launch config already covered by scanning the connected server?

Not the same information. A live tool-description scan sees what a server says about its tools after you have already launched it with whatever access the config granted. This checker looks at the grant itself, before that: the command, args, and env block that decide whether the server can read your filesystem, run a shell, or hold a secret in plain text in a file your client reads on every launch. A server can pass every tool-description check and still be launched with broader filesystem access, a less pinned version, or a hardcoded token than the config needed to grant.

Why would I need a config checker if MCP-Scan already exists?

Two reasons. First, what each one can see: MCP-Scan needs the server actually running and reachable, plus a call to an external API, to judge its tool descriptions; this tool needs only the config text you already have, checked entirely offline, before you decide whether to launch anything. Second, scope: this tool is not a tool-poisoning detector at all -- it never reads a tool description -- it is a structural audit of the launch grant itself, a question MCP-Scan's own documented scope does not cover.

Is this page affiliated with MCP-Scan or Invariant Labs?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Invariant Labs or the MCP-Scan project. MCP-Scan is an open-source security scanner, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, using facts drawn from its own public documentation and source repository at github.com/invariantlabs-ai/mcp-scan.

Check a config

It is not a security audit, and it does not replace reviewing your own config and each server's source before trusting it. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for meeting any obligation it helps you prepare for. Privacy. Everything runs client-side in your browser. The config you paste, and every finding this tool produces, never leaves your device -- there is no upload, no server-side processing, and no third-party analytics vendor.

vs-reading-the-config-by-hand.html.text:
← MCP Config Risk Check

MCP Config Risk Check vs. reading the config by hand

Reading a short config with one obviously broad command catches that command. It reliably misses a secret-shaped literal sitting under an unrelated key name, a missing version pin buried inside one of four different package-manager syntaxes, and a tool name that collides across two servers loaded together — which is what this free, no-upload checker computes exactly, in one pass.

Where reading it yourself stops being enough

Anyone approving a new MCP server already does this: open the config, read the command/args/env block, and decide whether it looks right. For a single server with a bare shell command or an obviously root filesystem path, that read catches it. The problem is the other checks below are not the kind of thing a skim of the rendered keys and values reliably surfaces, especially once a config carries more than a couple of servers.

What you're trying to confirmReading the config yourselfThis checker
A server's command is a shell interpreter, or an argument is exactly a root path like /, ~, or C:\.Works. This is the one case a plain read reliably catches.Also catches it, in the same pass as everything below.
An env value matches a real secret's shape (an sk- key, a ghp_/gho_ token, a Slack xox- token, an AWS AKIA key, a bearer token) sitting under a key not named token, key, or secret.Easy to skim past — a reviewer's eye is drawn to keys that look suspicious by name, not to every value's shape regardless of its key.Matched against every value against every known token shape, independent of the key name.
A package or image launched with no version pin, across npx, uvx, pipx run, and docker run — four different pin syntaxes in the same config.Requires remembering which syntax applies to which command while scanning every args array; easy to miss the one entry with no pin at all.Checked against each command's own pin syntax, the same way every time.
Whether a key named like a secret actually holds a live literal, versus a proper environment-variable reference such as "${MY_API_KEY}".The two read as visually similar strings in a JSON value; misreading one for the other is easy at a glance.Checked against the exact reference syntax, not just whether the value looks token-shaped.
A tool name exposed by more than one connected server, once the pasted data includes each server's own tool list.Requires holding every server's full tool list in mind at once and comparing them pairwise — manageable with two servers, unreliable past a handful.Compared exactly, name by name, across every server in the pasted data.
Re-checking an entire config again after adding or updating one server.One server at a time, remembered by hand, every time something changes.One paste, the whole config, every time.

A quick read is still the fastest way to catch an obviously broad command in a small config, and this checker is not doing anything a careful line-by-line audit couldn't — it is reading the same command/args/env blocks a careful audit would, just checking every value's shape and every pin syntax automatically instead of leaving the comparison to be remembered by hand.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: the browser page parses JSON you paste entirely in your own browser. It never sends your config anywhere.

Common questions

Can't I just read the config myself?

For a config with one or two servers and an obviously broad command like a bare shell launch, yes -- that case is visible on a single read. What reading does not reliably catch is a secret-shaped literal sitting under a key not named token or secret, a missing version pin buried inside one of four different package-manager argument syntaxes, or a tool name that collides between two servers loaded together. Those need every server's command, args, and env checked the same mechanical way, not remembered while skimming.

Why is spotting a hardcoded secret harder than it looks?

Because a reviewer scanning by eye naturally looks at keys named token, key, secret, or password and skims past the rest. A literal that matches a real secret's shape -- an sk- style key, a gh_-prefixed GitHub token, a Slack xox- token, an AWS AKIA access key, a bearer token -- can sit under any key name at all, including one that gives no hint. Confirming every value's shape against every known secret pattern, regardless of what its key happens to be called, is a pattern match across the whole config, not a read of the keys that look suspicious.

Why is a missing version pin easy to miss on a read-through?

Because npx, uvx, pipx run, and docker run each pin a version in a different place and syntax -- an @version suffix on a package name, a bare docker image without a :tag, or an argument list with no pin at all -- and a config with a dozen servers mixes all four. Holding four different pin syntaxes in mind while scanning a dozen args arrays, and noticing the one that has none, is exactly the kind of check that is reliable when it is the same mechanical comparison every time and unreliable when it depends on remembering which syntax applies to which command.

What about a tool name that collides across two servers?

That needs comparing every tool name a connected server exposes against every tool name every other connected server exposes -- not reading one server's config in isolation, but holding all of them in mind at once and checking for an exact match. With two servers and a handful of tools each this is manageable by eye; past a handful of servers it is the same kind of pairwise comparison a person does slowly and inconsistently and a check does exactly the same way every time.

Is this page making a live comparison against a tool or company?

No. This page describes a manual habit anyone approving an MCP server config already has -- reading the command, args, and env blocks by eye before trusting it. It names no competing product or company. The checker itself makes no network request of any kind: the browser page parses pasted JSON in your own browser, and nothing you paste is ever uploaded.

Want to know what a zero-finding scan actually means? Read why a clean scan isn't a safety guarantee.

why-a-clean-scan-isnt-a-safety-guarantee.text:
← MCP Config Risk Check

Why a clean scan isn't a safety guarantee

Zero findings means none of this tool's mechanical checks fired against the config you pasted — not that the servers you're about to launch are safe. Here is what a structural scan can and can't see, and why the difference matters.

What "structural" means here

Every check this tool runs looks at the shape of the launch config itself: is a server started with filesystem or shell access broader than it likely needs, is a secret written directly into the config instead of referenced from an environment variable, is a package or container image launched without a version pin so it can silently change on the next run, and do any two servers you've loaded together claim the same tool name. These are exactly the mistakes a careful human reviewer would look for by eye — mechanized so they don't get missed on a rushed review.

What it can't see

A structural scan has no way to know whether a pinned package version itself carries a known vulnerability or a supply-chain compromise, whether a server's actual runtime behavior matches what its tool descriptions claim, whether a description carries hidden model-directed instruction language, or whether a server that scanned clean last week was updated to something different since. Catching those needs a registry or vulnerability lookup, a tool that diffs a captured manifest against an earlier one over time, or a human reading the server's own source — not a one-time look at the config text.

This is the same reason a linter passing doesn't mean a test suite would: they check different, complementary things.

What a clean scan is worth, then

It rules out the specific, common mistakes above, cheaply, before you launch anything — worth running every time you add or change a server. Treat it as a floor: pair it with a version-pin habit, a registry or vulnerability check on anything unfamiliar, and a periodic re-scan after updates, rather than a one-time pass you never revisit.

Common questions

If a config scan comes back with zero findings, is the setup safe?

No. A zero-finding result means none of this tool's mechanical checks fired against the text you pasted — it does not mean the servers you're launching are safe. The scan looks at structure (broad filesystem or shell access, hardcoded secrets, missing version pins, duplicate tool names), not at what a server's code actually does when it runs, and it cannot see a vulnerability, a compromise, or a malicious update that hasn't yet shown up as one of those structural patterns.

What can a structural config scan actually catch?

Patterns visible in the launch config itself: a server started with broad filesystem or shell scope it may not need, a secret written directly into the config instead of referenced from an environment variable, a package or image launched without a version pin (so it can change under you on the next run), and tool names that collide or shadow each other across servers you've loaded together. These are the same category of mistake a careful human reviewer would look for — structural, not behavioral.

What can't it catch?

Anything that isn't visible as a pattern in the config text: whether a pinned package version itself contains a vulnerability or a supply-chain compromise, whether a server's actual runtime behavior matches what its description claims, whether a tool's description carries hidden model-directed instructions, or whether a server that looked fine yesterday was updated to something different today. Those need a registry/vulnerability check, a manifest-diff tool run over time, or a human reading the server's own source — not a one-time structural scan of the config.

So what is a clean scan actually worth?

It rules out the specific, common mistakes the scan checks for, cheaply and before you launch anything — the same value a linter has before a test suite runs. It is a floor, not a ceiling: worth running every time you add or change a server, and worth pairing with the practices that catch what it can't see, not a substitute for them.
